issues.issue: The election between separate-Principal and single-Principal treatment must be made by Agent "and the other party", but the default on failure to elect is stated only for a failure "to make such an election in writing". Whether an oral or implied election defeats the default rule is not addressed.

Clause (iii) requires margin under Paragraph 4 to be determined "on a Transaction-by-Transaction basis", whereas Paragraph 4(a) and 4(b) of the Agreement compute Margin Deficit and Margin Excess on the aggregate of all Transactions. The two calculation bases cannot both govern the same margin call.

Aggregate margin treatment here is made "subject to any greater requirement imposed by applicable law", an undefined override that no party is charged with determining. Which law and whose determination controls the margin figure is left open.

This deems both Agent and its Principals to be "parties" and treats any Act of Insolvency of the Agent as an Event of Default by Seller or Buyer, while Paragraph 3 of the same Annex IV insulates the Agent from guaranteeing Principal performance and from setoff. Whether the Agent is fully a party or a shielded intermediary is not resolved between the two paragraphs.

"Forward Exposure" is "the amount of loss a party would incur", "determined in accordance with market practice or as otherwise agreed by the parties", naming neither a determining party nor a method if market practice is contested. Every margin obligation under Annex V Paragraph 2 rests on this open figure.

Every Transaction whose Purchase Date has not yet occurred is a "Forward Transaction", so ordinary trades awaiting settlement fall under Annex V's separate collateral regime as well as Paragraph 4 of the Agreement. The overlap with Paragraph 11(a)'s cancellation of Transactions whose Purchase Date has not occurred is unaddressed.

Annex V margin rights are declared to be "in addition to their rights under subparagraphs (a) and (b) of Paragraph 4 and any other provisions of the Agreement", so the same exposure can be collateralised twice under two regimes. The collateral thresholds, the acceptability standard ("reasonably acceptable to the In-the-Money-Party") and the interaction with Paragraph 4 are left unreconciled.

Delivery is due by "the close of business in the relevant market" measured against the Margin Notice Deadline, both of which are undefined for Forward Collateral — Paragraph 2(i) of the Agreement ties the Deadline only to "market practice" absent agreement. Timeliness of a forward margin call is therefore unmeasurable on the text.

Return of Forward Collateral on settlement is defeated where the transfer "would result in the creation of a Net Unsecured Forward Exposure of the transferor", a figure the transferor itself computes under the open-ended Forward Exposure definition. The proviso can thus swallow the return obligation.

Each party here grants an outright security interest and right of setoff in Forward Collateral and "any other cash, Securities or property" transferred in connection with the Agreement, whereas Paragraph 6 of the Agreement creates only a deemed pledge conditional on Transactions being recharacterised as loans. The two describe different property arrangements over overlapping assets.

The Pledgee may rehypothecate Forward Collateral in amounts and for periods exceeding its entitlement, which is difficult to square with the Paragraph 3(a) characterisation of that same property as pledged security and with Paragraph 8 of the Agreement. What the Pledgor's residual interest is during such use is unstated.

An additional Event of Default arises for failing "after one business day's notice" to perform any obligation under this Annex, whereas Paragraph 11(iii) of the Agreement makes margin failures an immediate default without notice. Which applies where the same collateral failure can be framed under either is not resolved.

Liquidation of Forward Collateral is at prices the nondefaulting party "may reasonably deem satisfactory" in "a recognized market (or otherwise in a commercially reasonable manner)", or at a deemed credit price from a source of its own choosing. No standard fixes what is commercially reasonable for the collateral actually posted.

The replacement remedy again turns on prices the nondefaulting party "may reasonably deem satisfactory" or a deemed purchase at a price from a generally recognized source it selects, with no methodology. The internal roman numbering also restarts at (i)/(ii) inside subparagraph (ii), obscuring which election is being made.

The parties are deemed to acknowledge that all Forward Collateral consists of "instruments traded in a recognized market" and that the nondefaulting party may pick the pricing source "in its sole discretion". That deemed fact is at odds with the Market Value definition in Paragraph 2(j), which presupposes a source agreed by the parties.

Annex VI declares that its terms "prevail" over "any other term of the Agreement", which collides with Annex I Paragraph 2 (Annex I governs any inconsistency with the Agreement) and with the Annex VII preamble's identical claim to prevail. Nothing ranks the three supremacy clauses.

This requires that "[e]ach Transaction shall be identified... in the relevant Confirmation as either a Repurchase Transaction or a Buy/Sell Back Transaction", but the Confirmations actually issued under this Agreement are styled "Structured Repo Confirmation" and make no such election. What governs a Transaction that was never so identified is unaddressed.

Limb (i) refers to "the date originally specified by the parties as the Repurchase Date pursuant to Paragraph 2(q) of the Agreement", but Paragraph 2(q) is only a definition and specifies no date; the parties specify it in the Confirmation under Paragraph 3(b). The cross-reference misdirects the formula's central date.

Termination again turns on whether "the Repurchase Date is the date originally agreed to by the parties pursuant to Paragraph 2(q) of the Agreement", a paragraph that defines the term rather than fixing any date. Which Sell Back Price limb applies therefore rests on a faulty cross-reference.

Whether Purchase Price and Sell Back Price include Accrued Interest is switched by the undefined phrase "except to the extent contrary to market practice with respect to the Securities", which no party is charged with determining. The alternative formula applies or not according to that unfixed practice.

The paragraph presupposes agreement "in Annex I to the Agreement that a Buy/Sell Back Transaction is not to be repriced", but the executed Annex I contains no such provision, and "repricing" is nowhere defined or given a trigger. When repricing occurs, and on whose call, is left blank.

Annex VI Paragraph 9 disapplies Paragraph 5 of the Agreement to Buy/Sell Back Transactions and reverses the Income flow, while Annex I Paragraph 3 requires Buyer to pay Income to Seller under Paragraph 5(i) in any Transaction spanning an Income payment date. The two Annexes give opposite answers for the same payment.

The instruction that references to "Repurchase Price" "throughout the Agreement" be read as "Repurchase Price or the Sell Back Price, as the case may be" is unlimited on its face, reaching Transactions that are not Buy/Sell Back Transactions at all. "[A]s the case may be" supplies no rule for choosing between them.

The provision reads "In 11 of the Agreement", omitting the word "Paragraph", so the text being amended is identified only by a bare numeral. The mechanical omission leaves the scope of the substitution of "Repurchase Prices and Sell Back Prices" to inference.

The preamble makes the Agreement one "between Barclays Capital Inc. ('Counterparty') and each investment company identified on Schedule VII.A" — a schedule left blank — while declaring that Annex VII "shall prevail" over any other term of the Agreement. A supremacy clause for a party set that does not exist cannot be squared with Annex I Paragraph 2 or with the Barclays/Thornburg parties named in the Agreement.

Every reference to Buyer or Seller is to be read as a reference "solely to the particular Fund", yet no Fund is identified on Schedule VII.A and Thornburg is not an investment company. Applying this rewriting rule to an Agreement with no Fund would displace Paragraphs 4, 11 and 12 for no one.

This confines the Paragraph 4 margin obligations and "the single agreement provisions of Paragraph 12" to a single Fund's Transactions, directly cutting down Paragraph 12's declaration that all Transactions are one contractual relationship. The two cannot both govern the same set of Transactions.

Remedies are to be determined "as if each Fund had entered into a separate Agreement", a fiction that sits against Paragraph 11's aggregation of all Transactions on a single deemed Repurchase Date. Which frame governs a cross-Fund default is not stated.

The bar on setting off claims between Funds contradicts the express cross-Transaction setoff and netting right granted by Paragraph 12(ii) and (iii) of the Agreement. The conflict is left to be resolved by the unranked priority clauses in Annex I Paragraph 2 and the Annex VII preamble.

The operative number is a blank — "shall always be equal to at least _%" — leaving the Buyer's Margin Percentage for Fund-as-Buyer Transactions unfilled, with only the proviso of "not less than 100%" to supply content. An unfilled essential term in a margin provision is on its face indeterminate.

For Transactions in which a Fund acts as Seller the sentence still fixes "the Buyer's Margin Percentage", where the parallel structure and Paragraph 2(t) point to the Seller's Margin Percentage; as written the same percentage is set twice for opposite roles. The apparent drafting slip changes which margin amount the 100% floor protects.

Here the Counterparty alone "shall promptly issue a Confirmation", whereas Paragraph 3(b) of the Agreement puts the duty on "Buyer or Seller (or both), as shall be agreed". Who must confirm, and the effect of not doing so, differs between the two.

Each party "represents that it has delivered" specified financial information, yet the Agreement identifies no such delivery and the categories are keyed to a broker-dealer/Fund/other taxonomy that does not fit both signatories. A representation of past delivery that may be untrue feeds Paragraph 11(vi)'s default trigger.

The undertaking to deliver later statements "promptly upon request" sets no deadline and, for a party that is neither broker-dealer nor Fund, extends to "all such financial information that subsequently becomes available to the public" — an unbounded category. What must be produced, and when, is not fixed.

Transfers to a Fund must go to "the custodian or subcustodian designated for such Fund in Schedule VII.A hereto", but Schedule VII.A lists no Fund and no Custodian. The delivery mechanism has no designated recipient to operate on.

The schedule states that "[t]his Agreement is entered into by or on behalf of the following Funds" and then lists none, while Annex I Paragraph 1 makes the schedule part of the Agreement and Annex VII depends on it for the identity of the contracting parties. An incorporated but empty party schedule cannot be reconciled with the Barclays/Thornburg parties named on the cover.
